# ICMP reply fixtures

`echo_reply.bin` and `time_exceeded.bin` are raw bytes captured from a real
ICMP exchange on a live network, not hand-invented — same posture
`parse.rs`'s own fixtures take (built via `etherparse::PacketBuilder`
inline; these are real captured bytes instead because we needed to observe
actual OS ping-socket delivery behavior, not just construct a valid packet).

They were generated by `cargo run --example generate_icmp_fixtures`, which:

- opens a `SOCK_DGRAM`/`IPPROTO_ICMP` socket (the same unprivileged
  ping-socket mechanism `src/traceroute.rs` uses),
- sends an ICMP Echo Request with `IP_TTL=1` to a real external destination
  to elicit a genuine Time Exceeded reply from the first-hop router, saved
  as `time_exceeded.bin`,
- sends a second Echo Request at the default TTL to the same destination to
  elicit a genuine Echo Reply, saved as `echo_reply.bin`.

Both fixtures come back from `recv_from()` on this macOS version with a
leading 20-byte IPv4 header still attached, ahead of the actual ICMP
message — a long-standing BSD raw-socket quirk that applies to both message
types, not just error replies. `src/traceroute.rs`'s `parse_icmp_reply`
detects and strips this header before reading the ICMP type octet. This was
discovered empirically while first generating these fixtures — an earlier
version of this generator asserted `buf[0]` was the bare ICMP type and
failed immediately on the Time Exceeded case with `buf[0] == 0x45`.

To regenerate (e.g. if the reply format ever needs re-verifying against a
different macOS version): run `cargo run --example generate_icmp_fixtures`
from `capture-agent/`, from an unprivileged shell, with real network
connectivity. It overwrites both files in this directory.
